title: Eight Divisors of Thirty
statement: Let $N$ be the number of ordered $8$-tuples $(d_1, d_2, \dots, d_8)$ such that each $d_i$ is a positive divisor of $30$ greater than $1$ (repeated values are allowed) and the product $d_1 d_2 \cdots d_8$ is a perfect square. Find the remainder when $N$ is divided by $1000$.
hints: Fix $d_1, \dots, d_7$ and look at whether the exponents of $2$, $3$ and $5$ in their product are odd or even. What does this tell you about the possible values of $d_8$?

Use recursion on the length of the tuple. Let $a_k$ be the number of $k$-tuples of allowed divisors whose product is a perfect square, and build each $(k+1)$-tuple by appending one divisor to a $k$-tuple. A product is a square exactly when every prime exponent is even, so compare the exponent parities of the $k$-tuple's product with those of the appended divisor.

Each allowed divisor has exponents $0$ or $1$ at $2$, $3$ and $5$, and is not $1$. So a $k$-tuple with non-square product can be completed to a square product in exactly one way, and a $k$-tuple with square product cannot be completed at all. Since there are $7$ allowed divisors, this gives $a_{k+1} = 7^k - a_k$ with $a_1 = 0$. It remains to iterate this up to $a_8$ and reduce modulo $1000$.
solution: The allowed values are $2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15, 30$, so there are $7$ choices for each entry. Each of them is squarefree, with exponents $0$ or $1$ at the primes $2, 3, 5$, and every pattern of exponents occurs except all zeros. Let $a_k$ be the number of $k$-tuples of allowed values whose product is a perfect square. Then $a_1 = 0$, since no allowed value is a square. Fix a $k$-tuple with product $P$, which has only the prime factors $2, 3, 5$. For an allowed $d$, the product $P \cdot d$ is a square exactly when, for each of $2, 3, 5$, the exponent in $d$ has the same parity as the exponent in $P$. Since the exponents in $d$ are $0$ or $1$, this forces the exponent in $d$ to be $1$ at the primes where $P$ has an odd exponent, and $0$ at the others. So exactly one divisor of $30$ works. It equals $1$ exactly when all exponents in $P$ are even, that is, when $P$ is a square. Hence a $k$-tuple with non-square product extends to a square product in exactly one way, and a $k$-tuple with square product extends in no way. There are $7^k - a_k$ of the first kind, so $$a_{k+1} = 7^k - a_k.$$ Iterating from $a_1 = 0$ gives $$a_2 = 7,\quad a_3 = 42,\quad a_4 = 301,\quad a_5 = 2100,\quad a_6 = 14707,\quad a_7 = 102942,\quad a_8 = 823543 - 102942 = 720601.$$ So $N = 720601$, and the remainder when $N$ is divided by $1000$ is $601$. Why this works. recursion, perfect-square-exponent-parity: exponent parities force the only possible last entry, so each length's count follows from the one before.
